content: 1. Quality assessment involves evaluating the effectiveness, efficiency, and overall performance of health systems, ensuring that they meet established standards and objectives. 2. Estimates and projections are critical for forecasting future needs and outcomes, enabling informed decision-making and resource allocation. 3. In-depth studies are necessary to thoroughly investigate specific aspects of health systems, providing detailed insights and evidence-based recommendations. 4. The use of research results ensures that health programs and policies are grounded in reliable data and scientific evidence. 5. Assessing the progress, performance, and efficiency of health systems is essential to identify areas for improvement and to ensure that goals are being met effectively. 6. Targeted and comprehensive reporting provides detailed and specific information on health system performance, tailored to the needs of stakeholders. 7. Regular review processes are vital for continuously monitoring and evaluating health systems, ensuring that they remain responsive and effective. 8. Global reporting ensures alignment with international health goals and standards, facilitating collaboration and benchmarking across countries. 9. The construction of a national monitoring and evaluation framework should prioritize the use of SMART indicators—specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. 10. Indicators should align with those described in the national monitoring and evaluation framework for the health sector, as well as with global and regional targets for immunization. 11. Accurate baselines must be established to enable effective tracking of progress over time. 12. Targets should be realistic and achievable, taking into account baseline results and available resources. 13. National health information systems may not capture all the data needed to monitor the progress of comprehensive multi-year plans (cMYP) and sub-national plans. Additional data may need to be generated through field assessments, supportive supervision, or research studies. 14. Knowledge, attitude, and practice (KAP) studies can help identify barriers to access for high-risk groups, providing insights into how to improve service delivery. 15. Large population-based surveys, such as coverage surveys or demographic and health surveys, may be required to determine immunization coverage levels, reasons for non-immunization, gender barriers, and data disaggregation by location, sex, socio-economic status, and education level. 16. Mid-term and end-of-plan evaluations of the cMYP should be conducted to make mid-course corrections and inform the development of subsequent plans. 17. The program management system component of the cMYP should document the main strategies for monitoring progress toward immunization objectives, targets, and milestones, as well as evaluating the extent to which these goals have been achieved. 18. A monitoring and evaluation framework should identify key impact indicators (e.g., mortality), outcome indicators (e.g., program coverage), output indicators (e.g., system or program developments), and process indicators (e.g., achievement metrics) for the next plan period. 19. Planning systems at national and sub-national levels should include regular reviews of surveillance and coverage performance using standardized protocols to assess clinical, laboratory, and data management components. 20. An immunization research agenda should address information gaps to improve program performance, including studies on knowledge, attitudes, and practices; evaluations of new vaccine introductions; comprehensive program reviews; and assessments of vaccine logistics and management. 21. Financial sustainability strategies should be developed to address funding gaps, ensuring the reliable mobilization and efficient use of domestic and external resources to achieve immunization targets. 22. Costing the cMYP is a critical step in planning, providing essential financial information to achieve program objectives. This includes estimating current program costs, projecting future resource requirements, and identifying funding gaps. 23. Scenario-building can evaluate the cost and financing of alternative strategies to achieve program objectives, helping to identify the most feasible and cost-effective approaches. 24. Financial sustainability requires collaboration between governments and partners, emphasizing the need for reliable and efficient program funding. 25. Stakeholder engagement in the assessment and selection of financial sustainability strategies is crucial for generating new ideas and supporting the implementation of effective solutions.
